title: Biggest Odd Number at the Front
statement:
You get a string digits that is a large non-negative integer with no leading zeros. Consider every non-empty contiguous piece of it, read as a number.

Return the piece with the largest value among those that are odd, as a string. If no piece is odd, return the empty string "".

examples.why: The whole number already ends in an odd digit, and nothing longer exists.
The piece must end at an odd digit. The last odd digit is the 5, so the longest such piece is "35". "5" alone is odd too, but smaller.
Every digit is even, so every piece ends in an even digit.

constraints: digits has only 0–9 and no leading zeros
hints: Which digit decides whether a number is odd?
Every odd piece ends at an odd digit. Among pieces that end at the same place, which is the biggest?
Starting at index 0 gives the most digits, and a number with more digits (and no leading zeros) is bigger. So find the last odd digit and return everything up to it.

explain.intuition:
Only the last digit decides parity, so an odd piece must end on an odd digit. To be as large as possible, a piece should have as many digits as possible, because the input has no leading zeros: a longer piece starting at index 0 always beats a shorter one.

So the best piece starts at the very front and ends at the rightmost odd digit. Scan from the right, stop at the first odd digit, and return the prefix up to it. Converting to a number is never needed, which matters because the string can have 100 000 digits.
steps: Scan i from the last index down to 0.
pitfalls: Parsing the string into a number. 100 000 digits do not fit in any number type, and BigInt work is far too slow.
Returning the largest single odd digit. A longer prefix is always bigger.
Scanning from the left and stopping at the first odd digit, which returns a too-short piece.

solutions.title: Last odd digit from the right
solutions.idea: The answer is the prefix ending at the rightmost odd digit.

followups: Return the largest piece divisible by 5 instead. What changes?
Leading zeros are allowed and the answer must be returned without them. Does the greedy still hold?
